default.p.test-10-p1.outline.3.label: Vocabulary note
default.p.test-10-p1.outline.3.note: Explains the definition of the concept “wordplay” (言葉遊び) used in the passage.
default.p.test-10-p1.vietnamese:
Japanese people love wordplay. Many people probably tried games such as the “Tanuki Letter” when they were children. A tanuki is an animal resembling a dog. A letter written by a tanuki is understood as “ta-nuki,” meaning that you must remove “ta” before reading it. For example, a letter reading “ta-o-be-tan-tou-ta-wo-mo-ta-tte-ya-ta-ma-ni-i-ta-kou-ta” is read as “obentou wo motte yama ni ikou” (Let’s take boxed lunches and go to the mountains). Words that have the same pronunciation but different meanings are called homonyms, and the “Tanuki Letter” makes use of this. Besides “nuki” (remove), words with similar meanings can also be used. Why not try creating a letter like this yourself?

(Note) Wordplay: a game that makes use of the pronunciation or meaning of language.

default.p.test-12-p1.vietnamese:
Foreign visitors to Japan are often surprised to see realistic food models displayed at restaurant entrances. These sample food models are a distinctive aspect of Japanese culture, and today they have spread to countries in East Asia. When the food model looks delicious, people naturally feel like entering the restaurant. In addition, even when there are no food models, many restaurants in Japan provide menus with pictures, making it easy to order. This is because customers can clearly visualize the dishes.

Food models can be purchased in Kappabashi, Tokyo. Because they are unique and unusual, foreign visitors reportedly often buy them as souvenirs. There are also places outside Tokyo where people can experience making their own sample food models, and these places are said to be very popular with children.

(Note) Kappabashi: An area in Tokyo specializing in kitchenware and related items

default.p.test-18-p1.vietnamese:
At a New Year’s auction one year, a 342-kilogram bluefin tuna from Hokkaido was sold at Tokyo’s fish market for as much as 32.49 million yen. That works out to 95,000 yen per kilogram. A high-end sushi restaurant run by Japanese owners and a Hong Kong sushi chain jointly bid for and bought the fish. The Hong Kong chain’s Tokyo branch sold slices of otoro for 1,300 yen each, while the Japanese restaurant sold them for 2,500 yen each. Apparently, they would lose money unless they sold each piece for 9,000 yen. The Hong Kong executive said it was a customer-appreciation service, while the Japanese sushi restaurant seems to have bought it because of the feeling that “sushi is Japanese, so we cannot let foreigners beat us.” In any case, the event became a hot topic in newspapers and on television and was broadcast repeatedly, so if it is considered an advertising expense, I do not think it was an excessively expensive purchase.

（注釈 1）Successful auction bid: competing by offering purchase prices in order to acquire an item.

（注釈 2）Otoro: Toro is the fatty part of tuna. Otoro has the highest fat content and is the most expensive.

（注釈 3）1 kan: In the past, two pieces of nigiri sushi were counted as one kan, but today the term generally refers to one piece.

default.p.test-19-p1.outline.0.label: The problem of having no heir for the family grave
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.0.note: Describes the major problem of dealing with graves for elderly people in Japan because of family customs, a lack of heirs, and the declining birthrate.
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.1.label: The emergence and changing use of tree burials (Jumokusō)
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.1.note: Introduces tree burials, in which remains are buried beneath a tree, and explains that this practice is beginning to be adopted in cities rather than only in remote areas.
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.2.label: The outstanding advantages of tree burials
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.2.note: Analyzes the advantages of solutions to traditional grave problems: they save space, cost less, require no caretaker, and keep people close to nature.
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.3.label: The trend of keeping ashes nearby and diversifying ash-handling methods
default.p.test-19-p1.outline.3.note: Describes a new trend of keeping cremated remains in pendants or key rings, or turning them into diamonds, so that loved ones can always carry them.
default.p.test-19-p1.vietnamese:
What to do with one's family grave is a major issue for older people. In Japan, there is a custom whereby a family grave containing the remains of ancestors from several generations is inherited by the eldest son's family, while the families of second and third sons build new graves. Recently, an increasing number of people have graves but no one to inherit them. Because my friend is an only child, she had no choice but to move her parents' grave to her husband's family grave. Apparently, moving the grave cost a great deal of money. In the future, as the birth rate declines and the percentage of unmarried people rises, maintaining and caring for graves will become increasingly difficult. For these reasons, the number of people choosing tree burials has recently increased. This means being laid to rest beneath a tree. Until now, tree burials were usually carried out in places far from urban areas, making them inconvenient to visit. In recent years, however, tree burials have also begun to be offered in cities. Compared with conventional graves, tree burials require less space and are relatively inexpensive. In addition, no one needs to maintain or care for the grave. They also suit the desire to return to nature.

In addition, although they are not graves, pendants and key holders for keeping small pieces of a deceased person's bones close at hand are now being sold. Since these are simply containers, they cost around 30,000 yen. Furthermore, some people have begun having diamonds made from a deceased person's bones or hair so that they can wear them. Ways of handling cremated remains are becoming increasingly diverse.

default.p.test-2-p1.vietnamese:
Many people probably think that winter is a season when it is easy to gain weight. In fact, I often hear people say that they gain as much as 2 kg after the New Year holidays. In winter, people tend to exercise less because it is cold and they do not want to go outside. There would be no problem if we did not eat, but whenever we stay home, we end up eating something. According to one study, gaining weight in winter is actually quite strange, and winter is said to be the season when it is easiest to lose weight. This is because the amount of basal metabolic energy needed to keep the human body alive is greater in winter than in summer. Basal energy expenditure is 10% lower in summer than in spring and autumn, while in winter it is 10% higher. For this reason, winter can be said to be the ideal season for losing weight.

(Note) Basal metabolic energy: The minimum amount of energy required to sustain life.

default.p.test-20-p1.vietnamese:
Since 2009, ordinary citizens in Japan have begun participating in criminal trials. This is the lay judge system. However, it is said that about 1 in every 3 people summoned asks to withdraw. Cases in which withdrawal may be requested include illness or injury affecting the person or a family member, as well as circumstances such as a funeral, childbirth, or important work. Of approximately 18 people summoned, only 6 actually serve as lay judges (in addition, there are 2 alternate lay judges). As a result, some people are dissatisfied and argue that too many people are being summoned.

It is said that the daily allowance is less than 8,000 yen on the day lay judges are selected and less than 10,000 yen on days when they serve as lay judges. Regardless of whether people consider this amount large or small, some say that they would not want to participate no matter how high the payment was. ①This is because trials involving lay judges are not minor cases such as theft, but serious cases such as murder, and may sometimes involve imposing the death penalty, so some people say that they do not want to become lay judges. Since the judge and lay judges discuss the case together and reach a verdict by majority vote, lay judges also bear a great deal of responsibility. However, although the decision is made by majority vote, the agreement of at least one judge is always required. The reason is that with 3 judges and 6 lay judges, the lay judges alone could make the decision if an ordinary majority vote were used.

Thanks to the participation of ordinary citizens, penalties for crimes committed between family members tend to be lighter because of greater empathy, while sexual offenses tend to receive heavier penalties. Whether this is good or bad, verdicts seem to be gradually moving closer to the way ordinary people think. In addition, public interest in criminal trials is also increasing. Is this not the best outcome of all?

default.p.test-21-p1.vietnamese:
More than 20 years ago, I visited an NHK broadcasting station with an international student. In a small room, a 3D film was being shown. Without wearing glasses, simply by standing in a fixed position, I could see schools of fish and snowballs seeming to fly out toward me. Both the international student and I were extremely amazed by the 3D technology.

The mainstream 3D TVs today require viewers to wear special glasses. This is because they are made by using the difference between the images seen by the human right and left eyes. Movies adopted this technology early on to produce 3D works. The popularity of 3D films is increasing rapidly. However, it is still unclear how widely this type of 3D TV will spread. Recently, TVs that can display 3D images without glasses have also appeared on the market. Since viewers do not have to put up with the inconvenience of wearing glasses, this type seems likely to become more popular. It will certainly become a formidable competitor. Whichever type it is, the spread of 3D TVs will depend on how widely 3D programs are broadcast, unless their prices differ little from those of ordinary TVs. Apparently, large-scale 3D broadcasting has begun in the United States. In Japan, too, some television stations are broadcasting in this format. At the same time as 3D TVs for home use went on sale, electronics manufacturers also began selling 3D video cameras. If the cameras sell well, the TVs will sell as well. This is another influential factor.

(Note) NHK: Japan Broadcasting Corporation, an abbreviation of Nippon Hoso Kyokai. Japan's public broadcaster.

default.p.test-22-p1.vietnamese:
When someone does something for you, use the honorific pattern 「〇〇さんに～していただく」 (have someone do something for you). However, many people mistakenly use 「〇〇さんが～していただく」 (using the particle が incorrectly). If you want to use the particle 「が」, you must change the verb to 「〇〇さんが～してくださる」 (someone kindly does something for you). Foreign learners study this in class, and this topic is sure to appear on the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test. I worry that before long, foreign learners may use it more accurately than native speakers. Honorific language is taught in schools too, but students have not mastered it at all. From famous television presenters to people holding important positions in politics and business, even they use it incorrectly. Since people hear this almost every day on television, ordinary speakers have begun to think that this usage is correct. The other day, I heard someone wearing a sweater knitted by a friend say, “This sweater, my friend made it for me” (mistakenly saying '友だちが' instead of '友だちに'). I was astonished and wondered whether this confusion had really spread that far.

Language naturally changes over time. Both the phenomenon of dropping sounds (Note 1) and that of inserting extra sounds (Note 2) are, to some extent, unavoidable. Nevertheless, in Japanese, particles are the most important element. Japanese allows words that are understood from context to be omitted. This is possible because particles exist. If you cannot use particles correctly, you will no longer be able to use elliptical expressions. Isn't it time we did something to correct this situation?

(Note 1) The phenomenon of dropping 'ra': omitting 'ra' and saying 'tabereru' instead of the full form 'taberareru'.

(Note 2) The phenomenon of inserting 'sa': inserting 'sa' and saying 'yomasasete itadaku' instead of the correct 'yomasete itadaku'.

default.p.test-23-p1.outline.1.label: The fading spirit of “mottainai” and young people’s negative impressions.
default.p.test-23-p1.outline.1.note: Since the period of rapid economic growth, a disposable culture has caused Japanese people to lose the habit of cherishing objects. Young people raised in an age of abundance even regard this term as meaning “poverty” or “stinginess.”
default.p.test-23-p1.outline.2.label: The introduction of charges for shopping bags and young people’s reactions.
default.p.test-23-p1.outline.2.note: Although plastic bags now cost money, young people rarely bring their own bags. However, when attractive shopping bags appear, they eagerly use them, showing that young people are still willing to embrace items that are beautiful and stylish.
default.p.test-23-p1.outline.3.label: Using the traditional furoshiki cloth to spread the spirit of “mottainai”
default.p.test-23-p1.outline.3.note: The author proposes using the furoshiki—a convenient and attractive traditional cultural item praised by foreigners—to revive and spread the spirit of “mottainai,” with an explanation of what a furoshiki is.
default.p.test-23-p1.vietnamese:
Wangari Maathai, who won the Nobel Peace Prize, proposed making the Japanese word 「mottainai」 an international term, 「mottainai」. However, I think that the place that needs this word most right now may actually be Japan. Since the period of rapid economic growth, Japanese people have lost the attitude of valuing things—the spirit of 「mottainai」. This is because a disposable culture based on mass consumption has become widespread. For example, when a household appliance breaks down in Japan, people often simply buy a new one because repairs are too expensive. In addition, people who grew up in an affluent era throw away clothes as soon as they get a hole in them. In the past, people used old towels at home to make cleaning rags, but today they buy ready-made rags made from new towels. In the past, the word 「mottainai」 was associated with the positive image of treating possessions with care and appreciation. However, for many young people who grew up in an affluent period, the word has a negative image, suggesting things like 「poverty」 or 「stinginess」.

By the way, recently most supermarkets have begun charging for plastic bags. Some stores even offer a discount of about 2 yen if customers do not take a bag. Nevertheless, hardly any young people bring their own shopping bags. default.p.test-25-p1.outline.2.note: The passage compares traditional eating habits, which involved local seasonal foods, with modern habits, in which food is available year-round, and concludes that understanding the qualities of food is essential for maintaining health.

default.p.test-25-p1.vietnamese:
Some foods warm the body, while others cool it. Neither type is necessarily better than the other; for good health, it is best to consider the season and maintain a balanced diet. People living in hot regions need foods that cool the body, while those living in cold regions need foods that warm it. However, when someone is ill, it seems that in most cases the body should be warmed.

Basically, foods harvested in warm regions cool the body, while foods from cold regions warm it. The harvest season has a similar effect. Fruits and leafy vegetables grow above ground and therefore have a cooling effect, while foods that grow underground, such as onions and potatoes, warm the body. However, foods such as apples, cherries, and dried plums originated in cold regions, so rather than cooling the body, they warm it. Apples in particular are considered so healthy that they are said to make doctors unnecessary, and their lack of a cooling effect seems to be one reason. Foods that are dry and firm warm the body better than soft foods. Foods high in salt or spice also warm the body. Not all foods are classified into one of these two types; staple foods such as brown rice, corn, various tubers, and soybeans are said to belong to neither category.

In the past, people ate seasonal foods and foods harvested locally, so there was no need to worry about which foods warmed or cooled the body. Today, we can eat tomatoes and cucumbers all year round. Therefore, to maintain our health, we need to know in advance whether foods warm or cool the body.

(Note) Leafy vegetables: Vegetables whose leaves are eaten, such as spinach...

As we enter the age of internationalization, the number of people who study abroad to learn a language is increasing. Studying a language abroad does not simply mean learning the language of that country; it also means learning about the lives and customs of the people there. To someone you meet, you may be the first Korean person they have ever encountered. Your actions may shape their impression of the people of your entire country. Even if you are Mr. Kim, you will be seen as a "Korean," not as the individual Mr. Kim. If you do something good, Korea and Koreans will gain a good reputation; if you do something bad, they will be criticized. To put it dramatically, you become a representative of all Koreans.

On the other hand, you too will tend to judge the people of that country as a whole based on the people you meet. If you happen to meet a good person, you may think, "People from that country are so friendly," whereas if you happen to encounter someone unpleasant, you may think they are all terrible. This is perfectly natural. In reality, however, there is no such thing as a "typical Korean" or a "typical person from country XX". There are only individuals such as Mr. Kim, or, if they are Japanese, Mr. Yamada, and if they are British, Mr. Smith. During your long stay there, you will certainly realize this. You will understand that, just like in your own country, there are both good and bad people. However, except in special circumstances, people rarely have the opportunity to get to know many foreigners, so there is a risk that the impression you create will become fixed as a stereotype. That is why, when abroad, you must think very carefully before acting.

default.p.test-27-p1.vietnamese:
In the past, every autumn farmers hung corn under the eaves of their houses to use as seed for planting in the fields the following year. Nowadays, however, most farming households buy seeds from seed companies. This is because those seeds produce better-tasting crops, have stronger disease resistance, and yield more than home-produced seeds. However, they are what are called hybrid seeds, which cannot produce a next generation, so farmers must continue buying them every year.

For farmers, especially those in poor Asian countries, having to buy seeds every year is a major burden. In the Philippines, farmers opposed to "hybrid seeds" have begun exchanging seeds with one another. In Bangladesh, the purchase of "imported hybrid seeds" is provoking strong opposition from domestic seed researchers. Reports from Vietnam also indicate that although hybrid seeds are used, harvest yields increase only slightly, while hybrid seeds require a great deal of fertilizer, so profits ultimately increase hardly at all. Since most hybrid seeds in the world are owned by European and American companies, another problem is that money is increasingly being drained from poor countries.

I do not know whether hybrid seeds are truly good or not. Surely, some hybrid seeds are beneficial. But this is not a question of whether they are good or bad. The real problem is that companies control the rights to the seeds. Moreover, in many cases, the seeds are controlled by foreign companies. Is there a risk that they might stop selling them, or suddenly raise the prices sharply? Crops and fruit grow from seeds, and seeds are then produced from those crops and fruit; in this way, life continues to be passed on. This is the natural order. Although I know it will be difficult, I hope researchers will create high-quality seeds that can still maintain this natural cycle of life.

default.p.test-28-p1.vietnamese:
We often take baths to relieve fatigue. In reality, however, it is said that taking a bath instead increases the substance that causes fatigue. The reason baths are said to be beneficial is actually that they allow us to sleep soundly afterward. It is said that the best way to reduce the fatigue-causing substance is to close our eyes and remain still and quiet. In other words, sleep is the best solution. Naturally, taking a nap is also beneficial.

It would be ideal to have enough time to sleep every day, but that is difficult for busy people. So, if we get a full night's sleep even just once a week, will that effectively reduce the fatigue-causing substance? Surely everyone has experienced feeling even more tired after sleeping too much. This is said to be because, although the fatigue-causing substance has decreased, the feeling of fatigue remains. When we are so exhausted that the brain can no longer perceive fatigue, getting enough sleep causes the brain—which had previously been functioning sluggishly—to become active again and begin perceiving the fatigue. That is supposedly why we feel "even more tired instead."

In addition, it is said that hearing words of praise such as "You're working really hard" or "You saved me from a difficult situation" reduces the feeling of fatigue. Energy drinks and coffee have a similar effect. Eating something sweet is also beneficial. Feelings such as happiness and excitement reduce the sensation of fatigue. However, we must not forget that feeling refreshed again does not mean that the fatigue-causing substance has decreased.

There are also foods that are said to help reduce the fatigue-causing substance. Chicken breast is said to contain the greatest amount of a substance that has this effect. Migratory birds are said to possess this substance, which enables them to fly thousands of kilometers continuously without resting.

default.p.test-29-p1.outline.0.label: An unusual hiring method and a rule based on application order
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.0.note: The passage begins by discussing companies in Japan with unusual recruitment methods, leading to one company that hires applicants entirely in order of application, without examinations or interviews. This supports question 1.
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.1.label: Technological standing and a global customer network
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.1.note: Emphasizes that this is not an unknown company but a famous business that develops the world’s smallest gears and supplies precision components across all five continents.
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.2.label: Accepting an unusual applicant and achieving unexpected training results.
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.2.note: Unlike common practice, the company hires people rejected elsewhere for lacking qualifications, having questionable backgrounds, or dyeing their hair. They diligently learn the work and absorb knowledge, impressing the professors. Question 2 is based on this comparison.
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.3.label: The director's philosophy of developing people's abilities
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.3.note: The director’s view: companies that complain about a lack of talent actually lack the ability to nurture and train people; once recognized, people will develop their abilities on their own. Question 3 is based here.
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.4.label: Rules for free-form meetings and the two pillars of company development
default.p.test-29-p1.outline.4.note: The passage adds a rule allowing employees to decide freely whether to attend meetings and asserts that these two distinctive features support the company's growth.
default.p.test-29-p1.vietnamese:
There are many unusual companies in Japan. I hear that one company gives applicants fish to eat during recruitment and hires people who can eat the fish cleanly and neatly. Perhaps it is observing how skillfully they use their hands. But there is an even stranger company. It has no written tests or interviews at all. People join the company in the order in which they submit their applications. This is definitely not an unknown company. It is famous for having manufactured the world’s smallest gear, weighing one-millionth of a gram and measuring 0.14 millimeters in diameter. Its technical ability is highly regarded, so work orders pour in from all over the world. The company supplies tiny precision plastic components to places around the globe.

Normally, when recruiting employees, companies conduct written tests or interviews to learn about applicants carefully. This company, however, hires people without knowing anything about their education or background, which is truly astonishing. Could this cause problems? Most of the people who apply to this company appear to be people who would not be hired by other businesses. They are said to have been rejected for reasons such as lacking qualifications, having a troubled past, or dyeing their hair. Even these so-called “delinquents” are said to learn the techniques properly and work very hard. What is more, some are said to acquire so much knowledge that even university professors are amazed. According to the company president, when a business complains, “There are no capable people,” it is actually showing that the business lacks the ability to train people. Once people are recognized, they naturally demonstrate their abilities. People change, and the company gradually changes along with them. There is another astonishing rule here as well: employees are completely free to decide whether or not to attend meetings. Surely these two principles are the solid foundation supporting the company’s growth.

default.p.test-30-p1.outline.0.label: The background behind the idea of exporting clean vegetable factories
default.p.test-30-p1.outline.0.note: Japanese high-tech industries face difficulties because of price competition, so the company decides to integrate its technologies and sell a complete model of a clean vegetable factory.
default.p.test-30-p1.outline.1.label: The practical effectiveness and outstanding advantages of vegetable factories in Japan
default.p.test-30-p1.outline.1.note: The vegetable factory harvests once a month—more than four times the 2–3 annual harvests from fields. Its pesticide-free vegetables sell well, and it is highly successful in cold regions such as Hokkaido because it reduces transportation costs.
default.p.test-30-p1.outline.2.label: A plan to export complete vegetable-growing factories to deserts and cold regions
default.p.test-30-p1.outline.2.note: Solar panels, LED lights, lithium batteries, and a water-circulation system are integrated into one modular container for export to deserts and cold regions.
default.p.test-30-p1.vietnamese:
Today, fierce competition is taking place worldwide to develop and sell products such as solar power generators, LED lamps, lithium batteries, water purification equipment, and more. Japanese technology is among the best in the world in every respect. However, companies are constantly drawn into price competition and struggle with how to generate profits. Therefore, instead of selling each technology separately, they decided to bring to market a model of a clean-vegetable farm that integrates all of these technologies.

There are currently about 50 vegetable farms in operation in Japan. In open fields, vegetables can be grown only two or three times a year, but at these farms they can be harvested about once a month. Moreover, because the vegetables grown there do not use pesticides, they sell very well even if they are slightly more expensive. Since clean vegetables do not need to be washed either, they are very popular with restaurants. In cold regions such as Hokkaido, these farms are extremely effective. Transporting vegetables from distant warmer regions is expensive, whereas vegetables produced locally have low transportation costs and can compete fully on price.

They are planning to sell this vegetable-farm system to desert countries and cold regions. So that it can be used even in places without an electrical grid, they have installed solar panels on top and use low-power LED lamps instead of sunlight. They have also added lithium batteries to store the electricity generated and installed a circulation system to reduce water consumption. They put all these devices into a single container and sell it. This is the first time a vegetable-farm model has been exported. I am beginning to feel that this will succeed.

default.p.test-31-p1.vietnamese:
Estimated sales of publications issued in 2010 were approximately 1.87 trillion yen, down 3.1% from the previous year and marking the ninth consecutive year of negative growth since 1998. Estimated revenue exceeded 1 trillion yen in 1976 and 2 trillion yen in 1989, after which it began to decline about ten years later. Book and magazine sales peaked in 1996 and 1997, respectively. In addition, 57 publishers went bankrupt in 2009 because of the economic recession.

People are gradually shifting to reading news on computers and mobile phones. It is faster than printed newspapers and costs almost nothing. Recently, novels published on mobile phones have attracted considerable attention, with some mobile websites collecting as many as 1 million novels. Popular novels are also printed as books or made into films, so the publishing industry cannot afford to ignore them.

In 2010, the market for books read on mobile phones and personal computers (excluding magazines) was estimated at 65 billion yen, but it was predicted to grow to as much as 300 billion yen within a few years. Against this background, it is only natural that electronics companies would launch devices capable of reading many e-books. The year 2010 may be remembered in history as a turning point for this trend. E-book readers only 6 millimeters thick had already been launched. Equipped with functions similar to those of mobile phones—not only reading books but also reading newspapers, sending and receiving email, and downloading videos from the Internet—the devices were likely to be readily embraced by businesspeople. In the United States, e-books are said to cost only about one-third as much as traditional printed books, making them easy to purchase. Similarly, it is probably only a matter of time before e-books spread throughout the world.

(Note 1) Mobile-phone novel: a novel written or read using a mobile phone.

(Note 2) Video: moving images filmed with a movie camera, video camera, animation, or similar medium.

default.p.test-32-p1.vietnamese:
Perhaps no other bird is hated as much as the crow. I clearly remember a folktale that went something like this: when the birds were told that they could choose any color they liked, each species immediately decided on its own color, but the greedy crow could never make up its mind. The story says that while it kept saying that this color was beautiful and that one was beautiful, the crow eventually ended up completely black. Since I knew that mixing colors together would eventually produce black, I thought the crow was terribly foolish. Because I had assumed that crows were entirely black, I was very surprised when I saw crows in Russia that were both black and gray. I even thought they looked rather cute. At that time, I thought that perhaps black really was what had given crows such a bad impression.

The reason crows are hated is that they do things that cause people trouble and inconvenience. In cities, they tear open garbage bags in search of food, while in rural areas, they pull crops out of fields even when they are not looking for something to eat. Many people also know that crows place stones on railway tracks. Since this can lead to accidents, it is indeed an extremely difficult problem. Moreover, crows sometimes attack people to protect their young, making them dangerous.

Foreign students often say that Tokyo is full of crows. I do think that Tokyo has more crows than other cities. This is because the large amount of waste produced by shops means that the crows do not lack food. Tokyo is struggling because the crow population has increased too much. In the evening, when I see countless crows flying back to their nests, I sometimes feel frightened when I wonder how much further their numbers will continue to grow. In reality, although researchers consider crows to be highly intelligent and lovable birds, ordinary people's opinions may not change for the time being.

default.p.test-33-p1.vietnamese:
Many people probably write down their daily schedules in detail in a planner so that they can work or study efficiently. However, if they pack in too many plans, they may be unable to respond promptly when unexpected problems arise, and may even feel intensely stressed. An effective way to prevent this is to set aside "free time" in advance as part of the schedule.

For example, deliberately leave about one hour unscheduled each day. Then, even if an unexpected request comes up or work is delayed, you can use that time to make adjustments calmly. Moreover, if nothing goes wrong, you can use it to read or take a walk, allowing your body and mind to rest.

The purpose of schedule management is certainly not to fill every moment without a gap, but to carry out everything with peace of mind. Wouldn't deliberately including "time to do nothing" in your schedule ultimately improve both your daily efficiency and your quality of life?

default.p.test-34-p1.outline.0.label: The current state of and common beliefs about efficiency
default.p.test-34-p1.outline.0.note: Society favors speed and efficiency, creating a trend toward treating the elimination of free time as optimal.
default.p.test-34-p1.outline.1.label: The brain's scientific mechanisms and leisure time
default.p.test-34-p1.outline.1.note: Reverses the usual perspective: continuously forcing the brain to work exhausts ideas, while leisure allows the unconscious mind to organize and connect knowledge until a solution emerges.
default.p.test-34-p1.outline.2.label: The author's opinion and advice
default.p.test-34-p1.outline.2.note: Asserts that having spare time is essential preparation and advises proactively creating pauses to improve the quality of one's work.
default.p.test-34-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, efficiency and speed are demanded in everything, and more and more people stare at their smartphone screens, unwilling to waste even the smallest amount of free time. At first glance, people tend to think that completely eliminating wasted time is the best way to improve productivity.

However, some point out that if we are constantly exposed to information and keep our minds working without a break, it actually becomes harder for new ideas to arise. According to brain science research, it is precisely when we appear to be doing nothing—during “unstructured periods of leisure”—that we unconsciously reorganize past memories and knowledge and connect them with one another. For this reason, a solution that could not be found while struggling over a problem at a desk may suddenly come to mind while taking a walk or having a bath.

In short, “free time,” which may appear inefficient at first glance, is not useless time at all but an essential stage in preparing to deepen our thinking. Isn’t it ultimately the decision not only to be satisfied with filling our schedules with plans but also to actively create time to pause that leads to high-quality work and abundant ideas?

default.p.test-35-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, there is a growing emphasis on using time efficiently. Quite a few people constantly try to fill their spare moments (Note 1) with information—for example, reading the news on their smartphones while traveling, or listening to music or lectures while walking. At first glance, this may seem like a meaningful action that eliminates wasted time. However, if the mind is kept constantly active for a long period, wouldn't we lose the mental space needed for new ideas and deep thinking to emerge?

According to one study, it is precisely during "idle time," when we do nothing, that the human brain reorganizes the knowledge and memories it has acquired and connects information that seems unrelated. In short, the empty time that initially appears wasteful actually serves as an indispensable foundation for producing creative flashes of insight (Note 2).

Of course, this does not mean that pursuing efficiency is completely unnecessary. Appropriate time management is essential for carrying out daily work and study smoothly. However, rather than filling every moment with schedules or information, deliberately making room for "time spent doing nothing" in everyday life will certainly enrich both life and work.

（（Note 1））Spare time: the small amount of free time that appears between tasks or other busy activities.

（（Note 2））Flash of insight: an excellent thought or wonderful idea suddenly coming to mind.

default.p.test-36-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, thanks to the widespread use of digital technology, we can record and store enormous amounts of information at any time. As a result, people often tend to believe that effective learning and success at work come from storing in our minds all the knowledge we have ever heard or seen so that we will not forget it.

However, the human brain is not simply a data-storage facility. By forgetting things appropriately, we can avoid being bound by trivial information and extract only what is essential. If every minor memory from the past remained vivid, it would instead become more difficult to connect it with the information before us and think flexibly. In short, the mechanism of forgetting is not a defect of memory but an indispensable function for deepening thought.

Rather than valuing only the accumulation of knowledge, it is sometimes important to let go of unnecessary information. The mental space created in this way becomes the driving force for grasping the overall picture and giving rise to unique perspectives.

（(Note 1)）些細な (trivial, insignificant): describing something unimportant and extremely small.

In modern society, efficiency and speed are valued in every area, and there is a tendency to praise achieving many results in a short time. Even during breaks from work or studying, many people continue searching for new information on their smartphones, trying to use every spare minute efficiently. However, does keeping the mind constantly active and continually stuffing it with information really lead to creative achievements or deep thinking?

According to one study, it is precisely during periods of "daydreaming," when we are doing nothing, that the human brain reorganizes past memories and accumulated knowledge and unconsciously generates new ideas. Many people have probably experienced a good idea suddenly occurring while taking a walk or a shower. In other words, those seemingly useless periods of doing nothing are actually an important preparation stage for the brain's next deep thinking.

If pursuing greater efficiency too intensely causes us to lose the "space" in our minds and schedules, we may end up producing only stereotyped ideas that fit existing patterns. Could consciously stopping in daily life and daring to set aside time that produces nothing ultimately be the key to enriching our thinking and creating high-quality work?

default.p.test-38-p1.vietnamese:
In recent years, with the spread of smartphone scheduling apps, instantly entering and sharing schedules has become commonplace. However, while this kind of efficiency optimization is advancing, many businesspeople still deliberately continue to use paper planners. According to one survey, the most common reason people prefer paper planners is that 「writing down one’s schedule is itself time to put one’s thoughts in order」.

Digital tools excel at「recording information accurately and quickly」, but precisely because of this convenient speed, the process of deeply absorbing information and thinking it through tends to be omitted. By contrast, moving a pen across a handwritten planner involves a certain amount of「inconvenience」. Yet that very inconvenience gives us an opportunity to stop and think carefully about this week’s priorities and our future goals.

Modern people are constantly chased by time and tend to focus solely on how to minimize waste. But what truly matters is not simply speeding up our work; rather, is it not making sure we have time to reflect on our own actions and way of life? The paper planner teaches us the importance of taking a little extra time and care instead of being swept along by convenience.

（(Note 1)）Moving a pen: Writing smoothly and swiftly.

（(Note 2)）Putting in a little extra effort: Making a little extra effort or taking the time to explore and create.

default.p.test-39-p1.vietnamese:
In recent years, both in work and in study, there has been a tendency to value only 「efficiency」. People tend to regard reducing waste and achieving results in a short time as measures of ability. However, isn't it precisely the time spent taking detours or going through trial and error—things that may initially seem useless—that gives rise to new ideas?

For example, if we search for and act on the correct answer by the shortest route from the outset, we can obtain only the result we anticipated. On the other hand, while experimenting and failing, or reading books in unrelated fields, unexpected ideas may become connected. One survey also found that companies willing to devote part of their working time to free exploration had a higher rate of developing groundbreaking new products.

Of course, this does not mean denying the importance of carrying out routine tasks efficiently. However, instead of filling all the extra time created by improved efficiency with other tasks, deliberately setting that time aside as 「leisure」 without emphasizing a specific objective can be regarded as an essential attitude for long-term growth and creativity.

However, if they could see the results right in front of them, they might be able to persevere. We should calculate each day how much carbon dioxide we have reduced. The main amounts of carbon dioxide that can be reduced in one day are as follows: not taking a plastic bag reduces it by 42g; not leaving the television on continuously reduces it by 45g; not letting the shower run continuously reduces it by 86g; sorting garbage before throwing it away reduces it by 119g; setting the heater below 20 degrees reduces it by 129g; and taking the train, riding a bicycle, or walking instead of using a car can reduce it by 400g. default.p.test-40-p1.vietnamese:
Nowadays, whenever we do not understand something, we can immediately look it up on a smartphone, and the effort required to search for information has decreased considerably. At first glance, this saves time and seems to help us acquire knowledge efficiently. However, information obtained without any effort at all often disappears from our memory with astonishing speed.

According to one study, the process of reaching an answer through repeated trial and error (Note 1) and thinking provides strong stimulation to the brain and deepens understanding. In other words, actions that may appear inefficient, such as opening a book, checking the index (Note 2), and repeatedly turning to and fro between relevant pages, play an important role in firmly embedding knowledge.

Of course, digital search is undeniably convenient when we are in a hurry or want to confirm only a fact immediately. However, precisely because we live in an age when anything can be obtained easily, could deliberately retaining some "inconvenience" in daily life—taking the time to investigate things ourselves—help develop our ability to think deeply?

((Note 1)) Trial and error: Trying different methods, experiencing repeated failures, and finding the best approach.

((Note 2)) Index: A list that arranges keywords in the order of the 50-sound syllabary to make words easy to find in a book, while also showing the pages on which they appear.

default.p.test-41-p1.vietnamese:
Few countries are as rich in greenery and as extensively planted with trees as Japan. Whenever I looked at forests, I used to think that since they help prevent global warming, it would be better not to cut down trees. However, I have heard that old trees absorb less carbon dioxide. Therefore, old trees need to be cut down and replaced with newly planted ones. In 1995, Japan's forests were still young, but I have heard that if they are left as they are, there is a risk that they will eventually stop absorbing carbon dioxide altogether.

When a house is built with wood, the carbon dioxide contained inside the wood remains there. Therefore, it is desirable to make an effort to use Japanese wood to build houses and plant more new trees. Naturally, houses should also be kept in use for as long as possible, and if the wood can be reused when a house is demolished, it will not release carbon dioxide and will benefit the Earth's environment.

Japan's forestry industry has declined completely because of the increase in imports of inexpensive foreign wood. The self-sufficiency rate for wood, which reached as high as 86.7% in 1960, fell to 45.0% in 1970 and has remained at around 20% since 1995. The problem is not only the price. Japanese wood contains a great deal of moisture, so it is more prone to warping than imported wood and is reportedly more difficult to use. There is another problem as well. As timber prices have fallen, the people working in the mountains have become almost entirely elderly. Forests need to be thinned (Note 1) in order for trees to grow, but the number of people caring for Japan's forests has continued to decline, leaving the forests neglected.

When wood is used, it must be dried to prevent warping. Normally, natural drying takes three months or more. Naturally, this requires both time and money. Recently, artificial drying has become popular, and there are many different methods. Of these, drying the wood at a high temperature of about 100 degrees for two or three days is reportedly the most commonly used. However, drying wood at a high temperature causes it to crack and makes it difficult to produce strong, high-quality wood because the oil contained in the wood is lost. Moreover, the fuel costs required for the process are by no means small.

Recently, one company developed a low-temperature drying device. The device dries wood at 45 degrees for an entire week until its moisture content is reduced to about 10%. I have heard that this process prevents the wood from changing color and keeps its oil from escaping, making it possible to produce strong, high-quality wood. Since fuel costs are also kept low, the device is reportedly attracting a steady stream of visitors who come to see it.

I have the feeling that a faint ray of sunlight (Note 2) has begun to shine on Japan's forestry industry. I hope everyone will make full use of this device and work toward using more Japanese wood in order to prevent global warming.

(Note 1) Thinning: cutting down trees at appropriate intervals so that the remaining trees can grow well.

(Note 2) A faint ray of sunlight: weak sunlight shining through the clouds.

default.p.test-42-p1.outline.0.label: Introduction to the Miracle Apple and its challenger
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.0.note: Defines the miraculous apple as one grown without pesticides or fertilizer, explains its impossibility, and introduces Akinori Kimura.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.1.label: The arduous research process and a series of failures.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.1.note: Every attempt to eliminate the pests fails, the family’s finances fall to rock bottom, and only the family remains supportive.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.2.label: A turning point from forest land and success finally bearing fruit.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.2.note: Discover that forest soil is naturally soft and porous, imitate nature so microorganisms can live in the soil, and eventually produce apples.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.3.label: The remarkable properties of apples and Kimura's character
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.3.note: The flavorful apples do not discolor or rot; they sell out in 10 minutes at a low price, while Kimura stays busy giving talks and inspiring people.
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.4.label: The author's emotions and desire to share the story
default.p.test-42-p1.outline.4.note: The author admires Kimura's extraordinary efforts and wishes to share this inspiring story with everyone
default.p.test-42-p1.vietnamese:
“Miracle apples” are apples grown without pesticides and, moreover, without fertilizer. A “miracle” is something that normally cannot happen. It is said that growing rice or vegetables without pesticides requires tremendous effort, and producing completely pesticide-free crops is almost impossible. Apples, in particular, were said to be absolutely impossible to grow without pesticides. Yet one Japanese man dared to take on this challenge. His name is Akinori Kimura. He became so absorbed in his research that his records filled an entire box. Every year, he explored various creative ways to eliminate pests. At times, he even sprayed vinegar. But none of these methods worked. No matter what he did, the apple trees bore no fruit. Because he could not harvest a single apple and had no income, he was once forced to leave home and work as a laborer elsewhere. Naturally, his family’s life fell into extreme hardship. People around him called him a fool or a troublemaker, and even his relatives told him to give up. During this difficult period, only his family remained by his side and supported him. Even so, no matter how many methods he tried, the apples would not grow. In despair, he happened to notice that the soil in the forest was completely different from the soil in his garden: it was soft and well aerated, and the trees were full of vitality. He therefore studied forest soil and, hoping to create similar soil, let weeds grow freely and left the land in its natural state. Microorganisms then began living in the soil of his fields and orchards, making it soft and well aerated, just like the soil in the forest. The following year, the apple trees finally blossomed and bore fruit.

It is said that his apples have a very rich flavor. Ordinary apples change color immediately after being peeled or cut. His apples, however, reportedly retain their original color without discoloring. People even say that they do not rot. Naturally, they are extremely popular: as soon as they go on sale, they reportedly sell out in just ten minutes. Not everyone can buy them; only those who win a lottery ticket are allowed to purchase them. They cost ¥300 each. Compared with other apples, they are certainly not expensive. People believe that many would buy them even if the price were higher, but Kimura firmly refuses to sell them at a high price. This may be another one of his appealing qualities. Today, in addition to growing apples, he is busy providing agricultural guidance, giving lectures, publishing books, and more.

We cannot help being drawn to the unbelievably impoverished life he once endured, his countless experiments and efforts, his determination to continue facing challenges, and the success that ultimately came to him. We then want to share and spread his story so that others can learn about it as well. Since I myself am writing about his story, I have to admit that I am one of those people.

(Note) Microorganisms: organisms so tiny that they cannot be seen with the naked eye.

default.p.test-43-p1.outline.0.label: The decline of traditional shopping districts.
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.0.note: Describes how old shopping districts have lost customers because of population decline and competition from suburban supermarkets, becoming “shuttered shopping streets.” Evidence for Question 1.
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.1.label: Example 1: Opening free community classes in vacant spaces
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.1.note: The neighborhood uses vacant shops to offer free classes in health counseling, cooking, abacus calculation, and English to attract customers back.
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.2.label: Example 2: reconstructing a neighborhood in a nostalgic Showa-era style
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.2.note: The neighborhood overcame 30 years of decline by restoring its Showa-era scenery, and visitor numbers soared from 20,000 to 300,000.
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.3.label: Example 3: Incorporating fortune-telling into a neighborhood's business activities
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.3.note: The neighborhood invites a fortune-teller, sets up a daily fortune-telling stall, and local shops link fortune-telling with promotions. Basis for Question 2.
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.4.label: Lessons from successful cases and expectations for shopping districts nationwide
default.p.test-43-p1.outline.4.note: Conclusion: success comes from creative ideas and creating distinctive features that attract people to a locality. Evidence for question 3.
default.p.test-43-p1.vietnamese:
Customers are increasingly no longer visiting the old shopping districts that have existed for many years. This is because the population has declined, society has shifted to automobiles, and customers have been drawn away by large suburban stores. Shopping districts with many permanently closed shops keep their shutters down all the time, so they have come to be called “shutter streets.”

Some places decided that they could not continue this way and created distinctive shopping districts. One shopping district used vacant shops to offer free activities such as health consultations, cooking classes, parenting advice, abacus classes, and English conversation classes. Their aim was to attract local residents, even if only briefly. Thanks to these efforts, the number of visitors has reportedly begun to increase gradually.

Another shopping district overcame 30 years of decline by restoring a nostalgic row of buildings from the Showa era. Its visitor numbers, which had once peaked at only 20,000, have now risen to as many as 300,000. This is because not only local residents but also many tourists have started visiting. Young people from the cities have also returned, making the district increasingly lively.

There is also an interesting shopping district that uses fortune-telling as its theme. On one occasion, the district management invited 21 fortune-tellers. The event attracted far more female customers than expected and was covered by the media. With the intention of using this opportunity to revive the district, they built a “fortune-telling café” where people could have their fortunes told every day. In addition, on the fourth Friday of each month, they invite about 30 fortune-tellers to tell fortunes on the shopping street. They also ask local shops to link fortune-telling with their business activities. For example, a pub held a lucky draw using disposable chopsticks, and winners received a free glass of beer. An eyeglasses shop offered a 10% discount to winners. A butcher shop also introduced a “Great Fortune” fortune-telling croquette. As a result, both people who wanted a serious reading of their future and those who simply wanted to enjoy fortune-telling casually came one after another.

These examples show that every shopping district has creative ideas. Moreover, they are creating shopping districts that can attract large numbers of people, not just those from the local area. I sincerely hope that shopping districts across the country suffering from a lack of visitors will work together to develop good ideas and create attractive districts that showcase the unique character of their local communities.

((Note)) Great Fortune: the best possible luck

default.p.test-44-p1.outline.0.label: The current state of cancer treatment and the advantages of vaccines
default.p.test-44-p1.outline.0.note: The opening describes the rising number of cancer deaths, the physical burden of traditional treatments, and high expectations for a cancer vaccine with no side effects that would not require hospitalization.
default.p.test-44-p1.outline.1.label: How the vaccine works and the trial results
default.p.test-44-p1.outline.1.note: The passage explains in detail how lymphocytes destroy cancer cells through peptide injections and presents promising clinical-trial results in Japan.
default.p.test-44-p1.outline.2.label: Difficulties in research and a proposal for government funding support.

default.p.test-44-p1.outline.3.label: Notes on terminology in the passage
default.p.test-44-p1.outline.3.note: Explains specialized medical terms appearing in the passage: anticancer drugs, cancer vaccines, lymphocytes, and peptides.
default.p.test-44-p1.vietnamese:
The number of deaths from cancer worldwide continues to rise and is expected to soon become the leading cause of death. Cancer treatments include surgery, (Note 1) anticancer drugs, and radiation therapy, but all of these methods place a heavy burden on the body. Even when a cancerous tumor disappears or becomes smaller, the problem remains that the body is weakened. Research into (Note 2) cancer vaccines is currently under way, and vaccine treatment may avoid this problem. Since treatment consists simply of an injection, hospitalization is unnecessary and there are no side effects. Patients can receive treatment while maintaining their previous way of life.

Cancer develops when the body’s own cells change for some reason. We possess (Note 3) lymphocytes, whose function is to heal illness. Lymphocytes immediately begin attacking when a foreign substance enters the body from outside. However, although cancer cells are foreign, they are not attacked. Lymphocytes cannot recognize cancer cells as enemies because they originated from the body’s own cells after those cells changed. Apparently, a substance called a (Note 4) peptide is attached to cancer cells. Therefore, when a peptide is injected into the body, lymphocytes recognize the peptide as a foreign substance and begin attacking it. Naturally, they also attack cancer cells with peptides attached to them, because they recognize them as enemies. According to research in Japan, tumors became smaller in 20% of people who received the vaccine, while tumors remained the same size in 40%. Moreover, since all the participants had previously been diagnosed as terminal, the vaccine would presumably be even more effective for people in the early stages.

Nevertheless, it is also a fact that cancer-vaccine research in Japan has made little progress. Because the shape of a peptide differs depending on where the cancer develops, an enormous amount of research funding is needed to create vaccines for every type of cancer. In the United States, more than 500 billion yen can be spent each year on research. Donations from the public are also said to amount to a considerable sum. Japan, on the other hand, has only a few tens of billions of yen. The United States will certainly be the first to develop the vaccine. Some may argue that Japan could simply use that vaccine. However, using it in Japan would require multiple trials and government approval, which would take considerable time. More worrying still, the vaccine might not be effective for Asians, including Japanese people, because some medicines work differently depending on race. For this reason, Japan or Asia must develop its own vaccine at all costs. I hope the government will shoulder more of the cost of research. Developing a vaccine would save many lives and also help reduce the ever-increasing cost of medical care. Furthermore, exporting a new medicine would generate enormous profits. For the government, this would certainly not be a bad proposition.

(Note 1) Anticancer drug: A drug used in cancer chemotherapy.

(Note 2) Cancer vaccine: A drug used to prevent or treat cancer.

(Note 3) Lymphocyte: A cell responsible for preventing or healing illness.

(Note 4) Peptide: A type of protein formed from chains of linked amino acids.

default.p.test-45-p1.vietnamese:
Before the earthquake disaster, about 16 million Japanese traveled abroad each year, while approximately 8.61 million people visited Japan. More than 70% of these visitors came from Asia, with South Korea first, Taiwan second, and China third. Worldwide, the countries with the highest tourism revenues included the United States in first place at $110.1 billion, Spain in second at $61.6 billion, France in third at $55.6 billion, and Italy in fourth at $45.7 billion—mostly developed countries. In Asia, China ranked fifth and earned $40.8 billion. Japan ranked only 28th, earning $10.8 billion, but after the earthquake disaster, this declined sharply because of radiation concerns. In 2003, the government launched a tourism campaign called “Visit Japan.” It set a goal of attracting 10 million visitors a year by 2010, but failed to achieve it, and reaching that target seemed likely to remain impossible for some time. Even before the disaster, there were issues such as the strong yen and visa requirements, as well as inadequate consideration for tourists. In Japan, there were not even many signs in English, and if many tourists came from South Korea, there should have been more signs in Korean as well. From now on, Japan needs to promote itself as a long, narrow country with many wonderful scenic sites that remain completely unaffected by radiation.

Although tourist numbers were said to be low, Niseko in Hokkaido was still crowded with Australian skiers, while Akita was packed with South Korean tourists because of a Korean television drama. This resulted from the efforts of private organizations and local tourism departments. In other words, visitor numbers could be increased through creativity and the search for solutions. Fortunately, Hokkaido and Akita were not affected by radiation, so even if visitor numbers temporarily declined, they would probably recover.

Around the world, tourism is also being approached from different angles. South Korea and Singapore are focusing on medical tourism. Japan’s medical technology is by no means inferior, and it has a high prevalence of advanced equipment such as MRI scanners. Nevertheless, until recently, there were cases in which foreigners who wanted to come to Japan for treatment could not obtain visas and had to give up. South Korea, by contrast, even amended its medical laws to accept foreign patients. South Korea is famous for cosmetic surgery, but it also seems to hope to stimulate the tourism industry as a whole by increasing the number of patients in other medical fields. Today, countries popular as destinations for high-tech medical treatment at low cost include South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, and India. Thailand in particular attracted as many as 1.2 million medical tourists as early as 2005. Even without considering the effects of radiation, Japan seems likely to need considerable time to catch up with these countries.

Considering the current state of tourism in Japan, it can be said that although the country possesses many wonderful attractions, it has not yet made full use of them. To stimulate Japan’s tourism industry, I hope the government will also provide support with visa issuance so that ideas from private organizations and local communities can be successfully commercialized. Furthermore, while promptly resolving the nuclear power plant issue, it must actively communicate to the world that many areas have been completely unaffected by radiation. That is an important role for the government.

(Note 1) Earthquake disaster: a disaster caused by an earthquake. In this passage, it refers to the major earthquake and tsunami that struck eastern Japan in 2011.

(Note 2) Cosmetic surgery: surgery intended to improve appearance, such as nose augmentation or breast augmentation.

default.p.test-46-p1.vietnamese:
International product standards are extremely important. Products that fall outside established standards may cause no problem if sold only domestically, but they cannot be exported. Even paper has standard sizes. In Japan, the B series is commonly used, but the A series, originally a German standard, is used throughout the world. Even small components have international standards, and there are cases in which people cannot buy Japanese products even when they want to. No matter how excellent or inexpensive a product may be, one that does not conform to international standards cannot be sold. That is why every country wants its own products to become the standard. Being regarded as non-compliant with international standards would cause major losses for both companies and countries.

Until some time ago, there was no system like this, so it was enough simply to make good products. If a product sold well, its specifications would naturally become widely adopted. As a result, there was once fierce competition worldwide over standards for videotapes and DVDs.

However, under the international standards system, a good-selling or high-quality product does not necessarily become the world standard. World standards are decided according to the principle of one vote per country. At first glance this seems fair, but in reality political power has a considerable influence. International standards were originally promoted mainly around Europe. Since European countries are geographically close to one another, having different product specifications was extremely inconvenient. To solve this problem, they introduced standard specifications. Consequently, even today, world standards are largely decided under European leadership.

Although Japan possesses advanced technological capabilities, it still lags behind when it comes to securing international standards. Small and medium-sized businesses in particular have lost much of their overseas market without even knowing that such standards existed. Simply manufacturing products according to international standards cannot recover a lost market. What matters is how one approaches the issue and takes action. A switch made by one small or medium-sized company was selected as an international standard. It was a switch that turned on when pressed by hand, turned off when released, and cut the power when squeezed more tightly. It was an excellent product born from a natural human action: when people sense danger, they instinctively squeeze tightly. What matters is making active proposals for specifications and getting them adopted, as this company did.

In addition, when seeking to secure an international standard, it is necessary to build support among many countries willing to cooperate. China is one example. In China, products with its own specifications are manufactured for certain product categories and reportedly sell very well. Because it does not want to pay expensive patent fees, China uses different technology to manufacture products. This is possible partly because the country has a population of 1.3 billion. The Chinese market is so enormous that no country can ignore it. Today, there are cases in which China's position influences the adoption of standards. India may be the next country to hold such power. So what should Japan do politically? Simply insisting on the superiority of its technology is not enough. When seeking to establish a world standard, should Japan not continue proposing standards that benefit many countries?

default.p.test-47-p1.outline.0.label: The survival crisis of the Japanese press in 2009
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.0.note: The year 2009 marked an existential crisis for Japan’s press industry: many major publishers operated at a loss and accumulated heavy deficits as young people moved away from print newspapers and advertising revenue declined.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.1.label: The worldwide decline in the status of the press
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.1.note: The position of newspapers as a means of accessing information is declining worldwide, especially in South Korea and the United States, as the Internet continues to develop and overtake them.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.2.label: Bankruptcies and mass layoffs in the United States.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.2.note: In the United States, heavy dependence on advertising has caused numerous prestigious newspapers to go bankrupt or restructure and lay off reporters on a large scale.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.3.label: Efforts to address the crisis and the “new journalism” model.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.3.note: Discusses ways to overcome the crisis: charging for online news and the emergence of “new journalism,” in which unemployed reporters form NPOs to distribute news funded by donations.
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.4.label: The news industry’s risk of an all-encompassing crisis and solutions to save journalism
default.p.test-47-p1.outline.4.note: The author warns that the decline of newspapers will lead to a crisis throughout the information and communications industry and urgently calls for a system to support journalism.
default.p.test-47-p1.vietnamese:
2009 may go down in history as the year when the newspaper industry faced a crisis of survival. In Japan, the Mainichi and Sankei newspapers fell into financial decline, while the Asahi newspaper, the world's second-largest newspaper company, announced a huge financial deficit in its midyear financial report. The cause was the growing trend, particularly among young people, of turning away from print newspapers, which in turn led to declining advertising revenue. This was true of every newspaper company.

Around the world, newspapers were also losing their position as a means of accessing information. According to 2005 statistics, in Japan, 89% of people used newspapers as a source of information, compared with 44% who used the Internet. In South Korea at that time, the figures were 75.4% for newspapers and 65% for the Internet, showing that the Internet was rapidly catching up with newspapers. In the United States, the figures were approximately 65.2% and 65.3%, respectively, with the Internet slightly ahead. Internet use has grown even further since then, accompanied by a continuing decline in newspaper readership.

In the United States, even prestigious newspaper companies went bankrupt one after another. This was because American newspapers depended more heavily on advertising revenue than Japanese newspapers did. Excellent newspapers that had won the Pulitzer Prize many times also disappeared. Corporate restructuring and staff cuts were being accelerated. The New York Times made drastic staff cuts and reduced salaries as advertising revenue declined along with the economic recession. As a result, the number of reporters, which had been 60,000 in 1992, reportedly fell to only about 40,000.

To overcome this crisis, newspaper companies have been announcing plans to charge for online news one after another. In addition, a trend known as “New Journalism” has emerged, in which unemployed journalists establish nonprofit organizations (NPOs) to distribute news. In addition to selling news to generate revenue, they cover the shortfall through donations. The United States is a country where volunteer activities and charitable giving are very active. NPOs are also supported by people who engage in such activities.

Most of the news flooding the Internet today was originally produced by newspaper and television reporters who spent considerable time gathering information on site. Therefore, if newspapers decline, we may lose a way to understand what is happening in society. The news we read or hear today is not always gathered directly by the media organization presenting it. They must purchase missing reports from other media organizations. If there are only a few news sources, it becomes difficult to know the truth. This is extremely frightening. Who will pay for the news: the people who receive it, advertisers, or donations as in the United States? In any case, if newspapers continue to decline as they are now, the crisis in the newspaper industry will not stop with print media. Is this not precisely the time for us to create a system to support newspapers, the guiding light of society?

(Note 1) Pulitzer Prize: An award given in the United States for outstanding journalism and other achievements; it is regarded as the country's most prestigious award in these fields.

(Note 2) To distribute: To deliver news, articles, programs, and so on.

default.p.test-48-p1.vietnamese:
For people living in Japan—a country blessed with abundant water resources—it may be difficult to fully appreciate the claim that wars in the 21st century will be fought over water rather than oil. The Earth has approximately 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water, but about 98% of it is seawater. After excluding the water in glaciers and underground, the amount of water that can actually be used is only 1%. Today, many countries are struggling with water shortages. The world’s population is currently about 6.8 billion, and it is expected to reach 8 billion by 2025. Without countermeasures, water shortages may spread beyond those countries to Europe, Asia, and the United States. Water is needed not only for drinking. It is also essential for growing crops, so there is a risk of a food crisis as well.

Singapore is making the greatest effort to develop solutions to its water problems. In the past, it purchased more than 50% of its domestic water supply from Malaysia. However, when Malaysia demanded a price increase to 100 times the previous rate, Singapore decided to secure its own water supply. It is now launching a variety of projects, including water reuse, seawater desalination, and rainwater collection, while inviting companies and research institutes from around the world to work together on these projects. Singapore plans to supply 90% of its domestic water needs in the future and to sell the technologies it develops worldwide, earning enormous profits from the water business.

The water business covers a wide range of fields, from bottled drinking water and household water purifiers to water-supply and sewage equipment and seawater-desalination facilities. The market is worth tens of trillions of yen. Major corporations such as Veolia of France, Suez of France, and Thames Water of the United Kingdom are currently operating in more than 50 countries and reportedly control 70–80% of the market. These major corporations manage and operate everything, from constructing facilities and supplying water to collecting fees and treating wastewater. Japan is a world leader in technologies such as the membranes used to purify water and water pumps, but these technologies alone account for less than 1% of the entire water business. From a business perspective, companies need to offer comprehensive projects covering everything from water production to distribution, just like the major corporations do. The major corporations have long histories, while Japan has traditionally believed that water services should be handled by public organizations, so the field was not commercialized as it was in Europe. Since the sector was not opened to private companies until 2002, Japan still lacks experience in managing and maintaining facilities. This is why Japan has fallen behind the major corporations despite its advanced technology. Most seawater-desalination projects in oil-producing countries in the Middle East involving Japanese trading companies are joint projects with major water corporations. It is therefore not surprising that Veolia has finally begun operating water-purification plants and managing wastewater-treatment plants in Japan. To make up for Japan’s delay in the water business, a tremendous effort will be necessary.

default.p.test-51-p1.vietnamese:
1. Calling times: Do not make calls before business hours, during the lunch break, or after business hours, except in emergencies.

2. Answering the phone: Try to answer before the phone rings three times.

3. Identifying yourself: Clearly state your name using the format 「Yes, this is ○○ from North Corporation」.

4. Repeat the details of the matter once more to confirm them. You must also take notes.

5. Use honorific language and speak clearly and politely. Try to make a good impression.

Honorific language

・Adding 「san」 or 「sama」 to a company name or job title, as in 「Company XX-san」 or 「Department Manager XX-sama」, is incorrect honorific usage and should not be used, but sometimes it is unavoidable. Adapt flexibly depending on the other person.

・The honorific expression 「~ sashiageru」 is not grammatically incorrect, but some people find it unpleasant, so avoid using it whenever possible.

・A business partner’s company is called 「Onsha / Sochira-sama」, while one’s own company is called 「Tousha / Watakushidomo」.

・How to address a superior

Calls from outside the company: Use 「Department Manager OO」 or 「OO」; never add 「san」 after the name.

Within the company: Use the person’s title, such as 「Department Manager OO」 or simply 「Department Manager」.

Calls from a superior’s family member: Say 「Team Leader OO」 or simply 「Team Leader」.

6. (Note) Complaint calls: First apologize for causing trouble, listen carefully to what the other person wants to say to help them calm down, do not arbitrarily decide who is at fault, and thank them for calling.

7. Do not talk at length. Be careful not to say anything that might make the other person uncomfortable.

(Note) Complaint call: A call made to express dissatisfaction with a product or with someone’s attitude or behavior.

Ⅰ. Eligibility Requirements
（1）Applicants who have completed at least 12 years of formal schooling and are eligible to continue their education at higher-level schools in Japan.
（2）Applicants who have completed upper secondary school or hold a certificate or equivalent qualification indicating completion of upper secondary education.

Ⅱ. Application Documents
Student Documents
（1）Application for admission: 1 copy
（2）Personal history: 1 copy
（3）Study-abroad consent form: 1 copy
（4）Photographs (3 cm × 4 cm): 8 copies
（5）Diploma from the highest level of education completed (original) or certificate of graduation (if currently enrolled at a university, etc., a certificate of enrollment is also required): 1 copy
（6）Passport (photocopy): 1 copy (if available)
Documents for Financial Support
（1）Certificate of employment: 1 copy
（2）Bank balance certificate: 1 copy
（3）Certificate of annual income (for the previous year): 1 copy
（4）Document proving the relationship to the student: 1 copy
Please use the forms designated by the school for the application for admission, study-abroad consent form, and financial-support documents.

Ⅲ. Application Screening Fee
Please transfer 20,000 yen to the account designated by the school.

Ⅳ. Other: Applicants who are nationals of China, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Mongolia, Sri Lanka, Nepal, or Vietnam must submit additional documents in addition to those listed above. For details, please contact us by telephone, fax, or the internet.
